chunks: "Supply voltage is the biggest lever on all three. For power, dynamic power is proportional to V squared, so dropping the voltage 20% cuts dynamic power by 36%.

Leakage depends strongly on voltage too, since higher voltage raises subthreshold current through drain-induced barrier lowering and increases gate leakage, so leakage drops faster than linearly as I lower V.
For performance, the transistor's drive current depends on the overdrive, V minus the threshold voltage, so higher voltage means faster switching and a higher maximum clock frequency.
Delay goes roughly like V over (V minus Vt) to a power around 1. 3, so the gains flatten at high voltage, and near the threshold the circuit slows down dramatically.
Example: with a 0. 35 volts threshold, dropping from 0. 9 to 0.
72 volts reduces the achievable frequency by about 25%, but energy per operation drops 36%, and dynamic power drops about 52% once the clock comes down to what 0.
72 volts supports. Thermals follow from power: less power, less heat, junction temperature lower, and leakage drops further because of its temperature dependence.
So reducing voltage is the most effective way to reduce power and heat, as long as timing still closes.
The limits are on both sides: too low and SRAM becomes unstable and logic can't meet timing, too high and I risk oxide breakdown, aging like NBTI, electromigration, and a thermal blow-up.
That's why chips ship with voltage-frequency tables and guardbands."
